study.teach: A quarter note has a filled head and a stem, with no flag. In 4/4 it lasts one beat.
study.example: Say ONE, TWO, THREE, FOUR. Play one quarter note on each number. Those four notes fill one 4/4 bar.
study.prompt: How many beats does one quarter note last in 4/4?
study.hint: One note goes on each number.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long does this quarter note last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This sound lasts 1 beat.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, which note usually gets one beat?
checks.hint: The bottom 4 names a quarter-note beat.

study.title: Meet the half note
study.teach: A half note has a hollow head and a stem. In 4/4, we hold it for two beats.
study.example: Play once on 1. Keep holding on 2. Do not play a new sound on 2.
study.prompt: How many beats does a half note last in 4/4?
study.hint: Keep holding as you count 1, 2.

checks.prompt: Which picture would show a half note?
answers: A hollow head with a stem
A filled head with a flag
A hollow head without a stem
checks.hint: The half note has both a hollow head and a stem.

checks.prompt: You start a half note on beat 1 in 4/4. What should you do on beat 2?
checks.hint: Play the half note once, then hold it while you count both beats.

study.title: Whole and half notes
study.teach: A whole note has a hollow head and no stem. A half note has a hollow head and a stem.
study.example: In 4/4, a whole note lasts 4 beats. A half note lasts 2 beats. Two halves fill the same time as one whole.
study.prompt: Which note has a hollow head with a stem?
study.hint: Both heads are hollow. Look for the stem.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long does this whole note last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This sound lasts 4 beats.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long does this half note last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This sound lasts 2 beats.

study.title: Meet the eighth note
study.teach: An eighth note has a filled head, a stem, and one flag. Two eighth notes share one quarter-note beat.
study.example: In 4/4, count “1 &”. Play the first eighth on 1 and the second on &. Together they take one beat.
study.prompt: How many eighth notes fit one quarter-note beat?
study.hint: Say both parts: 1, &.

checks.prompt: An eighth note is written by itself. What parts do you expect to see?
answers: A hollow head and no stem
A filled head, a stem, and one flag
A filled head without a stem
checks.hint: A single eighth note has a filled notehead, a stem, and one flag.

checks.prompt: You play two eighth notes while counting “1 &”. When does the second note begin?
answers: At the same time as the first note
checks.hint: The first eighth starts on 1. The second starts on &, within the same beat.

study.title: Split a whole into halves
study.teach: One whole note can split into two equal half notes. Their total time stays the same.
study.example: In 4/4, the whole lasts 4 beats. Each half lasts 2. Two halves: 2 + 2 = 4 beats.
study.prompt: How many half notes match one whole note?
study.hint: Split the long note into two equal pieces.

checks.prompt: A whole note takes 4 beats in 4/4. After splitting it into two half notes, what is their total time?
checks.hint: Splitting changes the number of notes, not their total time: 2 + 2 = 4.

checks.prompt: The two halves of a whole note are equal. How long does each half last in 4/4?
checks.hint: Share the whole note’s 4 beats equally: each half gets 2 beats.

study.title: Split a half into quarters
study.teach: One half note can split into two equal quarter notes. The pieces still fill the same time.
study.example: In 4/4, a half lasts 2 beats. Two quarters last 1 + 1 = 2 beats.
study.prompt: How many quarter notes match one half note?
study.hint: One beat plus one beat fills the half note.

checks.prompt: Replace a half note with two quarter notes in 4/4. What happens to the total time?
checks.hint: Each quarter lasts 1 beat. Together they still fill 1 + 1 = 2 beats.

checks.prompt: Which is shorter in 4/4: one of the quarter-note pieces or the original half note?
checks.hint: One quarter lasts 1 beat, while the original half lasts 2.

study.title: Split a quarter into eighths
study.teach: One quarter note can split into two equal eighth notes. Two eighths still fill just one quarter-note beat.
study.example: The tree goes whole → half → quarter → eighth. Each branch splits one note into two equal shorter notes.
study.prompt: How many eighth notes match one quarter note?
study.hint: Each branch makes two equal pieces.

checks.prompt: When one quarter note splits into two equal eighth notes, each new note is…
answers: The same length as the quarter
checks.hint: Two equal shorter notes share the time that one quarter note used.

checks.prompt: Follow the rhythm tree: whole → half → quarter → ___. Which comes next?
checks.hint: Each branch splits a note into two equal shorter notes. Quarters split into eighths.

study.title: Beat and rhythm
study.teach: The beat is an even pulse. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences that fits around it.
study.example: Tap four even beats with your foot. Clap two quick sounds over one beat. The beat stays steady; the rhythm changes.
study.prompt: Which stays even while your clapping pattern changes?
study.hint: Your foot keeps the steady pulse.

checks.prompt: What is rhythm?
answers: A pattern of sounds and silences in time
checks.hint: Rhythm uses different lengths of notes and rests.

checks.prompt: What is the steady beat?
answers: The even pulse you can tap
checks.hint: The beat stays even while rhythms can change around it.

study.title: Count one note on each beat
study.teach: In 4/4, count 1, 2, 3, 4. Play a quarter note on each number.
study.example: Say 1, 2, 3, 4 evenly. Clap once on every number. Start the next bar at 1 again.
study.prompt: Which count matches four quarter notes in 4/4?
study.hint: There is one sound on each of the four numbers.

checks.prompt: You finish counting 1, 2, 3, 4 in a 4/4 bar. Which number starts the next bar?
checks.hint: Each new 4/4 bar starts its count at 1 again.

checks.prompt: You clap four quarter notes on 1, 2, 3, 4. How many claps go on each number?
checks.hint: A quarter note takes one beat here, so clap once on each number.

study.title: Keep counting while you hold
study.teach: A long note keeps sounding while the beats continue. Count each beat, but play the note only once.
study.example: A whole note in 4/4: play on 1 and hold through 2, 3, 4. Two half notes: play on 1 and 3.
study.prompt: What do you count while holding a whole note in 4/4?
study.hint: The sound stays on while all four beats pass.

checks.prompt: You begin a whole note on beat 1 in 4/4. Should you play it again on beats 2, 3, and 4?
answers: Yes, play again on every number
No, keep the same sound held
checks.hint: The beats keep passing, but the long note is played only once.

checks.prompt: Which beats start the two sounds when two half notes fill a 4/4 bar?
checks.hint: Hold the first sound through 1, 2. Start the second on 3 and hold through 4.

study.title: Count the space between beats
study.teach: To count eighth notes in 4/4, add “&” halfway between the beat numbers.
study.example: Say 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &. Keep the numbers even. Each & is halfway to the next number.
study.prompt: Which count matches two eighth notes on beat 1?
study.hint: One beat splits into the number and its &.

checks.prompt: Where does each & belong when counting eighth notes in 4/4?
answers: At the same time as a beat number
checks.hint: Keep the numbers steady. Each & falls halfway to the next number.

checks.prompt: Two eighth notes share beat 2. Which two syllables match them?
checks.hint: Use that beat’s number and then &: 2 &.

study.title: Keep the beat during silence
study.teach: A rest means stay silent for its length. Keep counting so the next sound starts at the right time.
study.example: In 4/4: play on 1, stay silent on 2, then play on 3 and 4. Your counting never stops.
study.prompt: What should you do during a rest?
study.hint: The sound pauses; the beat keeps going.

checks.prompt: A bar says: play on 1, rest on 2, then play on 3 and 4. Which number follows the silent 2?
checks.hint: The silent beat still counts as 2, so the next sound starts on 3.

checks.prompt: During a one-beat rest, what should your instrument do for that beat?
checks.hint: A rest fills time with silence. Keep the count moving while the instrument is silent.

study.title: Two flags make sixteenths
study.teach: A sixteenth note has two flags. Four sixteenth notes fit into one quarter-note beat.
study.example: Say “1 e & a” evenly across one beat. Each syllable gets one sixteenth note. Two beams can join the flags of grouped notes.
study.prompt: Which count splits beat 1 into four equal parts?
study.hint: Keep all four parts inside just one beat.

checks.prompt: A sixteenth note is written by itself. How many flags does it have?
checks.hint: A single sixteenth note has two flags.

checks.prompt: Grouped sixteenth notes can replace their flags with how many beams?
checks.hint: The two flags become two connecting beams when the notes are grouped.

study.title: Eighths and sixteenths
study.teach: Two eighth notes share one quarter-note beat. Four sixteenth notes share that same beat.
study.example: In 4/4, say “1 &” for two eighths. Say “1 e & a” for four sixteenths. An eighth lasts ½ beat; a sixteenth lasts ¼.
study.prompt: How many sixteenth notes fit into one quarter-note beat?
study.hint: Say all four parts: 1, e, &, a.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long does this eighth note last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This sound lasts ½ beat.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long does this sixteenth note last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This sound lasts ¼ beat.

study.title: Split, then count the pieces
study.teach: Each split makes two equal shorter notes. The pieces must still add back to the original length.
study.example: One whole = 2 halves = 4 quarters = 8 eighths = 16 sixteenths. One half = 2 quarters = 4 eighths = 8 sixteenths.
study.prompt: How many eighth notes last as long as one half note?
study.hint: A half lasts 2 beats. Each beat holds 2 eighths: 2 + 2.

checks.prompt: How many half notes last as long as one whole note?
checks.hint: Divide the longer written length into equal shorter notes: 2 half notes.

checks.prompt: How many quarter notes last as long as one whole note?
checks.hint: Divide the longer written length into equal shorter notes: 4 quarter notes.

study.title: Compare written lengths
study.teach: Whole, half, quarter, eighth, sixteenth: each next note lasts half as long as the one before it.
study.example: Whole: 4 beats. Half: 2. Quarter: 1. Eighth: ½. Sixteenth: ¼. To compare two notes, use their lengths, not how many symbols you see.
study.prompt: Which lasts longer in 4/4?
study.hint: One whole beat is longer than half a beat.

checks.prompt: Which shown note lasts longer in 4/4?
checks.hint: A whole note lasts longer than a half note.

checks.prompt: Which shown note lasts longer in 4/4?
checks.hint: A whole note lasts longer than a quarter note.

study.title: Flags and beams
study.teach: One flag or beam means eighth notes. Two mean sixteenths. Beams group notes for reading; they do not change the lengths.
study.example: Two beamed eighths still last ½ + ½ = 1 beat. Four beamed sixteenths still last ¼ + ¼ + ¼ + ¼ = 1 beat.
study.prompt: Does joining two eighth notes with a beam change their total length?
answers: No, it is still one beat in 4/4
study.hint: The beam helps your eyes group the notes.

checks.prompt: A beam joins short notes so they are easier to read; each keeps its length. Does beaming two eighth notes change their total length?
checks.hint: A beam groups notes so they are easier to read.

checks.prompt: One beam groups eighth notes. Two beams group notes half as long as eighths. Which notes are those?
checks.hint: Sixteenth notes have two flags or two beams.

study.title: A dot adds half
study.teach: A dot keeps the original length and adds half of it. It makes the note one and a half times as long.
study.example: Dotted half: 2 + 1 = 3 beats. Dotted quarter: 1 + ½ = 1½. Dotted eighth: ½ + ¼ = ¾.
study.prompt: What does a dot ADD to an eighth note in 4/4?
study.hint: The eighth already lasts ½ beat. Half of ½ is ¼.

checks.prompt: A dot adds half the plain length. A plain half note lasts 2 beats in 4/4. In 4/4, how long does this dotted half note last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This sound lasts 3 beats.

checks.prompt: A dot adds half the plain length. A plain quarter note lasts 1 beat in 4/4. In 4/4, how long does this dotted quarter note last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This sound lasts 1½ beats.

study.title: Rests can have dots
study.teach: A dot adds half the original length to a rest too. Stay silent for the entire dotted length.
study.example: A dotted half rest lasts 2 + 1 = 3 beats in 4/4. A dotted quarter rest lasts 1 + ½ = 1½ beats.
study.prompt: How long does a dotted quarter rest last in 4/4?
study.hint: Keep its original 1 beat, then add half a beat.

checks.prompt: A dot adds half the plain length. A plain half rest lasts 2 beats in 4/4. In 4/4, how long does this dotted half rest last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This silence lasts 3 beats.

checks.prompt: A dot adds half the plain length. A plain quarter rest lasts 1 beat in 4/4. In 4/4, how long does this dotted quarter rest last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This silence lasts 1½ beats.

study.title: Rests are measured silence
study.teach: A rest means silence for its written length. Matching note and rest names have equal lengths.
study.example: In 4/4: whole rest, 4 beats; half rest, 2; quarter rest, 1. Keep counting during silence. A whole-bar rest fills the entire bar.
study.prompt: Which lasts longer: a quarter note or a quarter rest?
study.hint: One sounds and one is silent. Both take one beat in 4/4.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long does this whole rest last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This silence lasts 4 beats.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long does this half rest last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This silence lasts 2 beats.

study.title: Small rests take time too
study.teach: An eighth rest is silent for half a quarter-note beat. A sixteenth rest is silent for a quarter of that beat.
study.example: Count “1 &”. Sound on 1, then stay quiet for an eighth rest on &. The next beat still arrives on time.
study.prompt: How long is a sixteenth rest in 4/4?
study.hint: A sixteenth rest matches a sixteenth note.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long does this eighth rest last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This silence lasts ½ beat.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long does this sixteenth rest last?
checks.hint: In 4/4, a quarter note gets one beat. This silence lasts ¼ beat.

study.title: Count the tiny pieces
study.teach: Four quarter-beat pieces make one beat. Two of those pieces make half a beat.
study.example: Think in sixteenths: ¼ + ¼ = ½. Add another ¼ to make ¾. Add the fourth ¼ to make 1 whole beat.
study.prompt: What is ½ beat plus ¼ beat?
study.hint: Two tiny pieces plus one tiny piece makes three of the four pieces.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long do these notes last altogether?
checks.hint: Add their lengths: 1 beat + ½ beat = 1½ beats.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long do these notes last altogether?
checks.hint: Add their lengths: ¼ beat + ¼ beat = ½ beat.

study.title: Add the lengths together
study.teach: To find a rhythm’s total length, add the length of every note and rest.
study.example: Half + quarter + eighth = 2 + 1 + ½ = 3½ beats. Quarter + two eighths = 1 + ½ + ½ = 2 beats.
study.prompt: How long is a quarter note plus two eighth notes in 4/4?
study.hint: The two eighths together make one more beat.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long do these notes last altogether?
checks.hint: Add their lengths: 1 beat + 1 beat = 2 beats.

checks.prompt: In 4/4, how long do these notes last altogether?
checks.hint: Add their lengths: 2 beats + 1 beat = 3 beats.

study.title: Fill the empty time
study.teach: A 4/4 bar holds four quarter-note beats. Subtract the used time to find how much is still empty.
study.example: Two eighths use 1 beat, leaving 4 − 1 = 3 beats. A half plus an eighth uses 2½, leaving 1½.
study.prompt: A 4/4 bar already has a half note and a quarter note. How much is empty?
study.hint: 2 + 1 = 3 beats used. Count up from 3 to 4.

checks.prompt: These notes start a 4/4 bar. How many beats are still empty?
checks.hint: A 4/4 bar has four quarter-note beats. 1 are filled, so 3 remain.

checks.prompt: These notes start a 4/4 bar. How many beats are still empty?
checks.hint: A 4/4 bar has four quarter-note beats. 1 are filled, so 3 remain.

study.title: A tie joins one held sound
study.teach: A tie joins two notes of the same pitch. Hold one sound for both lengths; do not play the second note again.
study.example: Half tied to quarter: hold for 2 + 1 = 3 beats. Quarter tied to quarter: hold for 1 + 1 = 2 beats.
study.prompt: How should two tied notes of the same pitch sound?
answers: One sound held for both lengths
study.hint: A tie says “keep holding”.

checks.prompt: A tie means keep holding instead of playing again. How should two tied notes of the same pitch sound?
answers: As one sound with their lengths joined
checks.hint: A tie means hold the first sound for both written lengths.

checks.prompt: A tie adds two same-pitch note lengths into one sound. In 4/4, a half note tied to a quarter note lasts how long?
checks.hint: Two beats plus one beat makes three beats.

study.title: Check which note gets the beat
study.teach: A quarter note gets one beat in 4/4. Other time signatures can use a different note for the main beat.
study.example: In 2/2, a half note gets one big beat. Two quarters share that beat. Written note lengths stay related in the same way.
study.prompt: Does a quarter note always get one big beat?
study.hint: Cut time counts half-note big beats.

checks.prompt: Which note gets one big beat in 2/2?
checks.hint: Cut time counts half-note big beats.

checks.prompt: In 2/2, two quarter notes together share how many big beats?
checks.hint: Two quarters equal one half note, and the half note gets one big beat in 2/2.

time-signatures.title: Time signatures
time-signatures.intro: Learn how beats make bars, then explore different beat groups.

sections.title: The same time in smaller pieces
Fill bars & count more than one bar

steps.prompt: How many beats fit in this bar?
steps.teach: A bar is a group of beats. Count four taps.
steps.hint: Count the four boxes.

steps.prompt: Which note gets one beat here?
steps.teach: This is a quarter note. It gets one beat here.
steps.hint: The picture shows a quarter note.

steps.teach: Put one quarter note on each beat.
steps.hint: Tap Add note four times.

steps.prompt: How many little parts fit here?
steps.teach: These six little sounds travel in two groups.
steps.hint: Count all six boxes.

steps.prompt: How many BIG beats do you feel?
steps.teach: Feel two big beats: ONE-la-li, TWO-la-li.
steps.hint: Tap on ONE and TWO.

steps.teach: Put three eighth notes here. Put three there.
steps.hint: Fill both groups of three.

steps.prompt: Which note gets one BIG beat here?
steps.teach: Cut time has two big beats. Each is a half note.
steps.hint: The picture shows a half note.

steps.teach: One half note for ONE. One for TWO.
steps.hint: Tap Add note twice.

study.title: Music comes in bars
study.teach: A bar is a group of beats. A bar line marks its boundary. Start the next full bar’s count at ONE.
study.example: In 4/4: 1, 2, 3, 4 | 1, 2, 3, 4. The line separates bars; it does not tell you to stop playing.
study.prompt: What does a bar line mark?
study.hint: It separates one group of beats from the next.

checks.prompt: What does a time signature help organize?
checks.hint: A time signature tells us how written time groups into bars.

checks.prompt: What does a bar line show?
checks.hint: A bar line separates one bar from the next.

study.title: Find the time signature
study.teach: Look near the clef at the start. The top number counts the written note units in a bar.
study.example: 2/4 has 2 quarter-note units. 3/4 has 3. 4/4 has 4. 2/2 has 2 half-note units. 6/8 has 6 eighth-note units.
study.prompt: Which number tells you there are three quarter-note units in 3/4?
study.hint: Read the number above the other number.

checks.prompt: What is the top number of 2/4?
checks.hint: Read the number above the other number.

checks.prompt: What is the top number of 3/4?
checks.hint: Read the number above the other number.

study.title: The bottom names a note value
study.teach: The bottom number names the written unit: 2 means half note, 4 means quarter note, and 8 means eighth note.
study.example: The bottom 8 in 6/8 names eighth notes. It does not mean eight beats or eight seconds. Three eighths can group into one big beat.
study.prompt: Which written note value does the bottom 2 name?
study.hint: Think of a whole note split into 2 equal halves.

checks.prompt: Which written note value does the bottom 4 name in 2/4?
checks.hint: The bottom number names the written note unit: 2 = half, 4 = quarter, 8 = eighth. In 6/8, three eighths group into each big beat.

checks.prompt: Which written note value does the bottom 4 name in 3/4?
checks.hint: The bottom number names the written note unit: 2 = half, 4 = quarter, 8 = eighth. In 6/8, three eighths group into each big beat.

study.title: Two quarter-note beats: 2/4
study.teach: In 2/4, each quarter note gets a beat. A full bar has two quarter-note beats.
study.example: Count ONE, two | ONE, two. Two quarter notes fill one bar. Four eighth notes fill the same time.
study.prompt: How many quarter notes fill one 2/4 bar?
study.hint: The top 2 counts two quarter-note units.

checks.prompt: How many eighth notes fill one 2/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 2 quarter notes, which equals 4 eighth notes.

checks.prompt: How many sixteenth notes fill one 2/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 2 quarter notes, which equals 8 sixteenth notes.

study.title: Three quarter-note beats: 3/4
study.teach: In 3/4, feel three quarter-note beats in each bar. Each beat can split into two eighth-note parts.
study.example: Count ONE, two, three. Three quarters fill the bar. A half note plus a quarter does too: 2 + 1 = 3.
study.prompt: Which notes fill one 3/4 bar?
answers: A half note and a quarter note
study.hint: A half takes two quarter-note beats. Add one more.

checks.prompt: How many quarter notes fill one 3/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 3 quarter notes, which equals 3 quarter notes.

checks.prompt: How many eighth notes fill one 3/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 3 quarter notes, which equals 6 eighth notes.

study.title: Four quarter-note beats: 4/4
study.teach: In 4/4, a full bar holds four quarter-note beats. Notes of different lengths can share the bar.
study.example: Count ONE, two, three, four. Two halves fill one bar: 2 + 2 = 4. Eight eighth notes fill the same time.
study.prompt: Is a 4/4 bar containing two half notes full?
study.hint: Each half lasts two quarter-note beats.

checks.prompt: How many quarter notes fill one 4/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 4 quarter notes, which equals 4 quarter notes.

checks.prompt: How many eighth notes fill one 4/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 4 quarter notes, which equals 8 eighth notes.

study.title: Keep counting through rests
study.teach: A bar can mix notes and rests. Silence still uses written time; keep counting so the next note starts correctly.
study.example: In 4/4: quarter note, quarter rest, half note. Their lengths are 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 beats: a complete bar.
study.prompt: Does a quarter rest use space in the bar?
answers: Yes, the same written length as a quarter note
Only when the music is loud
study.hint: Count its silence before starting the next sound.

checks.prompt: Can a bar include both notes and rests?
checks.hint: Add the lengths of sounds and silences to fill the bar.

checks.prompt: During a rest, do you still count the beats in the bar?
checks.hint: Rests take time too, so keep the pulse going.

study.title: Two half-note beats: cut time
study.teach: 2/2 is called cut time. Its sign can be a C with a vertical line. Each half note gets one big beat.
study.example: Count ONE-and, TWO-and. Two half notes fill the bar. Each big beat holds two quarters, so the bar holds four quarters altogether.
study.prompt: Which note gets one big beat in cut time?
study.hint: The bottom 2 names the half-note beat.

checks.prompt: How many quarter notes fill one 2/2 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 4 quarter notes, which equals 4 quarter notes.

checks.prompt: How many eighth notes fill one 2/2 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 4 quarter notes, which equals 8 eighth notes.

study.title: Two groups of three: 6/8
study.teach: A 6/8 bar has six eighth-note parts, usually grouped 3 + 3. That makes two big beats.
study.example: Say ONE-la-li, TWO-la-li. Each big beat holds three eighths: one dotted quarter. Two dotted quarters fill the bar.
study.prompt: How many big beats do we usually feel in 6/8?
study.hint: Feel ONE and TWO; la-li are the smaller parts.

checks.prompt: How many quarter notes fill one 6/8 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 3 quarter notes, which equals 3 quarter notes.

checks.prompt: How many eighth notes fill one 6/8 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 3 quarter notes, which equals 6 eighth notes.

study.title: Count equal written lengths
study.teach: One quarter note has the written length of two eighth notes. Count the same amount of time using smaller pieces.
study.example: A 2/4 bar: 2 quarters = 4 eighths. A 3/4 or 6/8 bar: 3 quarters = 6 eighths. A 4/4 or 2/2 bar: 4 quarters = 8 eighths.
study.prompt: How many eighth notes fill one 3/4 bar?
study.hint: Each of its three quarters can split into two eighths.

checks.prompt: How many eighth notes fill one 2/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 2 quarter notes, which equals 4 eighth notes.

checks.prompt: Which group fills one 2/4 bar?
checks.hint: Compare written lengths. 2 quarter notes fill this bar even if you feel a different big beat.

study.title: Count sixteenth-note pieces
study.teach: One quarter note has the written length of four sixteenths. This relationship stays the same in every meter.
study.example: A 2/4 bar holds 8 sixteenths. A 3/4 or 6/8 bar holds 12. A 4/4 or 2/2 bar holds 16.
study.prompt: How many sixteenth notes fill one 6/8 bar?
study.hint: Six eighths can each split in two: 6 × 2.

checks.prompt: How many sixteenth notes fill one 2/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 2 quarter notes, which equals 8 sixteenth notes.

checks.prompt: How many sixteenth notes fill one 3/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 3 quarter notes, which equals 12 sixteenth notes.

study.title: Written length and the big beat
study.teach: When comparing bars, use the same written unit. A quarter-note length is useful even when a quarter is not the big beat.
study.example: A cut-time bar has two big half-note beats but four quarter-note lengths. A 6/8 bar has two big beats but three quarter-note lengths.
study.prompt: How many quarter-note lengths fit one 6/8 bar?
study.hint: Pair its six eighths into three pairs.

checks.prompt: How many quarter notes fill one 2/4 bar?
checks.hint: This bar holds the written length of 2 quarter notes, which equals 2 quarter notes.

checks.prompt: Which group fills one 2/4 bar?
checks.hint: Compare written lengths. 2 quarter notes fill this bar even if you feel a different big beat.

study.title: Find the empty written length
study.teach: Find the bar’s full written length, then subtract what is already used. Count notes and rests the same way.
study.example: A 4/4 or 2/2 bar holds 4 quarter-note lengths. If 3 are used, 1 remains. A 3/4 or 6/8 bar holds 3; use 2, leaving 1.
study.prompt: A 3/4 bar already uses two quarter-note lengths. How much remains?
study.hint: Its total is 3. Subtract the 2 already used.

checks.prompt: A 2/4 bar already holds ½ quarter-note length. How much more written length fits?
checks.hint: The bar holds 2 quarter-note units. Subtract the amount already filled.

checks.prompt: A 2/4 bar already holds 1 quarter-note length. How much more written length fits?
checks.hint: The bar holds 2 quarter-note units. Subtract the amount already filled.

study.title: Fill half-length spaces
study.teach: Half a quarter-note length is one eighth. Two half-length pieces join to make one whole quarter-note length.
study.example: A 4/4 bar with 1½ quarter-note lengths used has 2½ left: 1½ + 2½ = 4. A 3/4 bar with 1½ used has 1½ left.
study.prompt: A 6/8 bar holds 3 quarter-note lengths. If 1½ are used, how much remains?
study.hint: Two equal groups of 1½ make 3.

checks.prompt: A 2/4 bar already holds ½ quarter-note length. How much more written length fits?
checks.hint: The bar holds 2 quarter-note units. Subtract the amount already filled.

checks.prompt: A 2/4 bar already holds 1½ quarter-note lengths. How much more written length fits?
checks.hint: The bar holds 2 quarter-note units. Subtract the amount already filled.

study.title: Fill the last tiny spaces
study.teach: A quarter of a quarter-note length is one sixteenth. Four of those tiny pieces make one quarter-note length.
study.example: A 2/4 bar holds 2 quarter-note lengths. If 1¼ is used, ¾ remains. Count three tiny pieces: 1¼ → 1½ → 1¾ → 2.
study.prompt: A 2/4 bar has used 1¼ quarter-note lengths. How much remains?
study.hint: Count three more tiny pieces to reach 2.

checks.prompt: How many sixteenth-note pieces make one quarter-note length?
checks.hint: Each tiny piece is ¼ of a quarter-note length. Four pieces make one whole quarter-note length.

checks.prompt: A 2/4 bar has used 1½ quarter-note lengths. How much written time is left?
checks.hint: Count from 1½ to 2: another ½ quarter-note length finishes the bar.

study.title: Two full bars
study.teach: For two bars, add one bar’s written length twice. Their beat grouping can stay different even when their totals match.
study.example: Two 2/4 bars: 2 + 2 = 4 quarters. Two 3/4 or 6/8 bars: 3 + 3 = 6. Two 4/4 or 2/2 bars: 4 + 4 = 8.
study.prompt: How many quarter-note lengths fill two complete 3/4 bars?
study.hint: One bar holds 3. Add another 3.

checks.prompt: Two complete 2/4 bars last as long as how many quarter notes?
checks.hint: Each bar holds 2 quarter-note lengths. Two bars hold 4.

checks.prompt: Two complete 3/4 bars last as long as how many quarter notes?
checks.hint: Each bar holds 3 quarter-note lengths. Two bars hold 6.

study.title: Compare complete bars
study.teach: Compare quarter-note lengths, not just top numbers. Two quarters are shorter than three, and three are shorter than four.
study.example: 2/4 holds 2 quarter-note lengths. 3/4 and 6/8 hold 3. 4/4 and 2/2 hold 4. Use these totals to compare any pair.
study.prompt: Which complete bar has more written note length: 2/4 or 6/8?
study.hint: Compare their totals: 2 quarter-note lengths and 3.

checks.prompt: Which complete bar has more written note length: 2/4 or 3/4?
checks.hint: Compare quarter-note lengths: 2/4 holds 2; 3/4 holds 3. The felt beat can still differ.

checks.prompt: Which complete bar has more written note length: 2/4 or 4/4?
checks.hint: Compare quarter-note lengths: 2/4 holds 2; 4/4 holds 4. The felt beat can still differ.

study.title: Same length, different beats
study.teach: 4/4 and 2/2 bars have equal written length. Their main beats are grouped differently.
study.example: Both hold four quarter notes. In 4/4, feel four quarter-note beats. In 2/2, feel two half-note big beats.
study.prompt: Do 4/4 and 2/2 bars hold the same written note length?
answers: No, 2/2 always holds twice as much
No, 4/4 always holds twice as much
study.hint: Both bars hold the written length of four quarters.

checks.prompt: How many main beats do you feel in a 2/2 bar?
checks.hint: In 2/2, the two main beats are each a half note long.

checks.prompt: Four quarter notes fill a 4/4 bar. Can those same four written quarters also fill a 2/2 bar?
answers: Yes, grouped into two half-note big beats
No, 2/2 needs twice as many quarters
No, 2/2 needs half as many quarters
checks.hint: Both bars hold four quarter-note lengths. Their main-beat grouping is different.

study.title: 3/4 and 6/8 feel different
study.teach: 3/4 and 6/8 bars have equal written length, but their usual beat grouping is different.
study.example: Both hold six eighths. In 3/4: three beats, each split in 2. In 6/8: two big beats, each split in 3.
study.prompt: Which description matches the usual grouping?
answers: 3/4: three groups of two; 6/8: two groups of three
study.hint: Say 1-& 2-& 3-&; then say 1-la-li 2-la-li.

checks.prompt: Which complete bar has more written note length: 3/4 or 6/8?
checks.hint: Compare quarter-note lengths: 3/4 holds 3; 6/8 holds 3. The felt beat can still differ.

checks.prompt: Do 3/4 and 6/8 have the same usual beat grouping?
answers: No: 3 beats of 2 parts versus 2 beats of 3 parts
checks.hint: Both fit six eighth notes, but their grouping is different.

study.title: Grouping is not speed
study.teach: Time signatures group written time. Tempo controls how quickly the chosen beat moves. Cut time does not automatically double the speed.
study.example: You can feel slow or fast half-note beats in 2/2. Look for the tempo instruction to know how quickly to count ONE, TWO.
study.prompt: Does 2/2 always mean “play twice as fast as 4/4”?
answers: No, it must be twice as slow
study.hint: The time signature groups the beats. The tempo sets their speed.

checks.prompt: Does 2/2 require the music to be played twice as fast as 4/4?
answers: No, it must be twice as slow
checks.hint: The time signature organizes beats; tempo sets how fast the chosen beat moves.

checks.prompt: Which part of music tells you how quickly to feel the beat?
checks.hint: Tempo sets speed; the time signature sets grouping.

major-minor-keys.title: Major & minor keys
major-minor-keys.intro: Find a home note, follow a scale, then build more patterns.

sections.title: Build a major scale & number its notes

steps.guide: A key gives music a home note.
steps.caption: This little tune comes home to C.
steps.hint: The tune starts and ends on C.

steps.guide: A scale is a ladder of notes in a key.
steps.caption: C major: up to C, then back down.

sounds.label: Hear C major go up and down

steps.hint: The notes climbed, then came back home.

steps.guide: Major and minor can have the same home.
steps.caption: C major and C minor both come home to C.
steps.hint: Both names begin with C.

steps.guide: Change E to E-flat. Hear a different colour.
steps.caption: E-flat (E♭) is the piano key just left of E.

sounds.label: Hear C major: C E G
Hear C minor: C E-flat G

steps.hint: The minor example uses E-flat: E♭.

steps.guide: Major often sounds bright. Minor can sound mellow or dramatic.
steps.caption: Either kind can make happy or sad music.
steps.prompt: Can minor music sound happy too?
steps.hint: Music has many moods. Major and minor are not mood rules.

steps.guide: The same kind of scale can start somewhere else.
steps.caption: D major uses D as its home.
steps.hint: The first part of a key’s name tells its home note.

steps.guide: Minor scales can start on different home notes too.
steps.caption: This is A natural minor.
steps.hint: A minor comes home to A.

steps.guide: The same notes can have different homes.
steps.caption: C major and A minor share notes. Their homes are different.
steps.prompt: Do these keys have the same home?
steps.hint: Look at the glowing home notes: C and A.

study.title: A tune has a home
study.teach: A key gives music a home note. The tune often feels settled when it comes back to that note.
study.example: C major comes home to C. A minor comes home to A. Start by listening for where a tune feels finished.
study.prompt: What is the home note of C major?
study.hint: The first part of the key name tells its home.

checks.prompt: What is the home note of A minor?
checks.hint: The first part of A minor’s name is its home note: A.

checks.prompt: A tune returns to one note and feels settled or finished. What might you have found?
checks.hint: A key gives music a home, and returning there often feels settled.

study.title: Find the home note
study.teach: The home note is called the tonic. Read the first part of a key’s name to find it.
study.example: D major comes home to D. B-flat minor comes home to B-flat. The home letter repeats higher or lower.
study.prompt: What is the tonic of F-sharp minor?
study.hint: Keep the whole first note name, including its sharp or flat.

checks.prompt: What is the home note of C major?
checks.hint: The first part of the key name names its home note: C.

checks.prompt: What is the home note of A minor?
checks.hint: The first part of the key name names its home note: A.

study.title: Follow the letter ladder
study.teach: Scale letters move A, B, C, D, E, F, G, then start again. Keep each note’s printed sharp or flat.
study.example: A major shows A B C-sharp D E ? G-sharp. The missing letter is F. Of the offered choices, choose the F-sharp answer.
study.prompt: Which letter comes next in E, F, G, …?
study.hint: After G, the music letters start again at A.

checks.prompt: Follow the letter names A–G, then repeat. Fill the missing note in this C major scale.
checks.hint: The C major notes are C, D, E, F, G, A, B.

checks.prompt: Follow the letter names A–G, then repeat. Fill the missing note in this G major scale.
checks.hint: The G major notes are G, A, B, C, D, E, F-sharp.

study.title: Small steps and bigger steps
study.teach: A half step reaches the very next piano key, including black keys. A whole step takes two half steps.
study.example: C → C-sharp is a half step. C → C-sharp → D is a whole step. E → F is a half step: no black key sits between them.
study.prompt: How many half steps make one whole step?
study.hint: Take two next-key moves to make a whole step.

checks.prompt: Follow the letter names A–G, then repeat. Fill the missing note in this C major scale.
checks.hint: The C major notes are C, D, E, F, G, A, B.

checks.prompt: Follow the letter names A–G, then repeat. Fill the missing note in this G major scale.
checks.hint: The G major notes are G, A, B, C, D, E, F-sharp.

study.title: Read the whole note name
study.teach: A sharp raises a note one half step. A flat lowers it one half step. Both change pitch.
study.example: C-sharp is the next piano key above C. E-flat is the next key below E. Include black keys when finding the next key.
study.prompt: What does D-sharp mean?
study.hint: Sharp means the next piano key higher, not a change in loudness.

checks.prompt: Follow the letter names A–G, then repeat. Fill the missing note in this C major scale.
checks.hint: The C major notes are C, D, E, F, G, A, B.

checks.prompt: Follow the letter names A–G, then repeat. Fill the missing note in this G major scale.
checks.hint: The G major notes are G, A, B, C, D, E, F-sharp.

study.title: Keep the home, change the colour
study.teach: Major and minor can keep the same home. Changing a note can change the musical colour.
study.example: C major uses C E G. C minor uses C E-flat G. E moves down a half step, while C stays home.
study.prompt: What changes C E G into C E-flat G?
study.hint: Compare the middle note. E becomes E-flat.

checks.prompt: Compare C major, C E G, with C minor, C E-flat G. Which note changed?
answers: The middle note E became E-flat
checks.hint: Lowering the middle E to E-flat changes this C major sound into C minor.

checks.prompt: If a melody changes from C major to C minor, does its home letter have to change?
checks.hint: Parallel major and minor keys share the same home note.

study.title: Music has many moods
study.teach: Major often sounds bright; minor can sound mellow or dramatic. Neither one has to match a single mood.
study.example: A minor tune can be lively. A major tune can be gentle or sad. Speed, loudness, and many other choices help make the mood.
study.prompt: Must every minor piece sound sad?
study.hint: Major and minor are musical colours, not rules for one emotion.

checks.prompt: Must every major piece sound happy?
answers: No, major music can have many moods
checks.hint: Mode is one part of musical colour. Tempo, dynamics, and other choices affect mood too.

checks.prompt: Must every minor piece sound sad?
answers: No, minor music can have many moods
checks.hint: Minor can sound many ways, including lively or dramatic.

study.title: Build a major scale
study.teach: A major scale follows whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. These are distances between neighboring scale notes.
study.example: C major starts C → D: whole; D → E: whole; E → F: half. Its full ladder is C D E F G A B C.
study.prompt: In C major, is E → F a whole step or a half step?
study.hint: E and F are neighboring piano keys. That is one half step.

checks.prompt: Follow the letter names A–G, then repeat. Fill the missing note in this C major scale.
checks.hint: The C major notes are C, D, E, F, G, A, B.

checks.prompt: Follow the letter names A–G, then repeat. Fill the missing note in this G major scale.
checks.hint: The G major notes are G, A, B, C, D, E, F-sharp.

study.title: Count the home as one
study.teach: Number a shown scale from its home. The first note is 1, the next is 2, and so on.
study.example: C D E F G A B becomes C=1, D=2, E=3, F=4, G=5, A=6, B=7. Keep sharp and flat names when counting.
study.prompt: With C counted as 1, what number is A?
study.hint: Touch each note once: C 1, D 2, E 3, F 4, G 5, A 6.

checks.prompt: The relative natural minor starts on note 6 of a major scale. Count the first note as 1. C major has which relative minor key?
checks.hint: The relative minor starts on the sixth note of the major scale: A.

checks.prompt: Count the home as 1. What is the third note of the C major scale?
checks.hint: Count from the home note as 1: C, D, E.

study.title: Find the third note
study.teach: To find a scale’s third note, count its home as 1. This works for both major and natural minor.
study.example: G major begins G A B, so B is third. A natural minor begins A B C, so C is third. Read the supplied scale.
study.prompt: D major begins D, E, F-sharp. Which is its third note?
study.hint: Count D as 1, E as 2, and F-sharp as 3.

checks.prompt: Count the home as 1. What is the third note of the C major scale?
checks.hint: Count from the home note as 1: C, D, E.

checks.prompt: Count the home as 1. What is the third note of the A natural minor scale?
checks.hint: Count from the home note as 1: A, B, C.

study.title: Same notes, a new home
study.teach: A major key and its relative natural minor share notes. The minor’s home is note 6 of the major scale.
study.example: C D E F G A B: count C as 1. A is note 6, so C major and A minor share notes. Their homes differ.
study.prompt: G major is G A B C D E F-sharp. Which relative minor starts on note 6?
study.hint: Count G 1, A 2, B 3, C 4, D 5, E 6.

checks.prompt: The relative natural minor starts on note 6 of a major scale. Count the first note as 1. C major has which relative minor key?
checks.hint: The relative minor starts on the sixth note of the major scale: A.

checks.prompt: The relative natural minor starts on note 6 of a major scale. Count the first note as 1. G major has which relative minor key?
checks.hint: The relative minor starts on the sixth note of the major scale: E.

study.title: Make a three-note chord
study.teach: A triad is a three-note chord. Use notes 1, 3, and 5 of a scale.
study.example: C major: C D E F G. Notes 1, 3, 5 are C E G. In C minor, the third is E-flat: C E-flat G.
study.prompt: Which notes make the C major triad?
study.hint: Count the major scale: C 1, D 2, E 3, F 4, G 5.

checks.prompt: Compare C major, C E G, with C minor, C E-flat G. Which note changed?
answers: The middle note E became E-flat
checks.hint: Lowering the middle E to E-flat changes this C major sound into C minor.

checks.prompt: Which notes make a C major triad?
checks.hint: C major uses C, its major third E, and G.

study.title: Check the shown notes
study.teach: To check whether a note belongs, look through the supplied scale. Compare its full name, including sharp or flat.
study.example: D major shows D E F-sharp G A B C-sharp. F-sharp is in the list. F natural is not: F and F-sharp are different notes.
study.prompt: D major shows D E F-sharp G A B C-sharp. Which note is outside this scale?
study.hint: Look for the complete note name. The list has F-sharp, not F natural.

checks.prompt: Use the shown notes. Which note is NOT in the C major scale?
checks.hint: The scale is C, D, E, F, G, A, B. C-sharp is outside this collection.

checks.prompt: Use the shown notes. Which note is NOT in the G major scale?
checks.hint: The scale is G, A, B, C, D, E, F-sharp. C-sharp is outside this collection.

dynamics.title: Dynamics: loud & soft
dynamics.intro: Learn a few loudness signs, then practise changing the sound.

sections.title: Very soft, very loud & the middle
Follow the signs & listen to the group

steps.guide: Dynamics means how loud or soft music is.
steps.caption: Same tune. Same speed. Different loudness.
steps.hint: Dynamics tells us how loud or soft to play.

steps.guide: Piano means soft. Its music sign is p.
steps.caption: p = piano = soft
steps.hint: Piano starts with p. It means soft.

steps.guide: Forte means loud. Its music sign is f.
steps.caption: f = forte = loud
steps.hint: Forte starts with f. It means loud.

steps.guide: Double the letter for very soft or very loud.
steps.caption: pp = pianissimo: very soft. ff = fortissimo: very loud.
steps.hint: Two p signs make pianissimo: very soft.

steps.guide: Mezzo means moderately. These levels sit in the middle.
steps.caption: mp = mezzo piano: moderately soft. mf = mezzo forte: moderately loud.
steps.hint: Mezzo forte: moderately loud. Look for mf.

steps.guide: Crescendo means grow louder little by little.
steps.caption: The opening sign shows the sound growing.
steps.hint: Keep the same beat. Let the sound grow louder.

steps.guide: Diminuendo means grow softer little by little.
steps.caption: Also called decrescendo. The sign closes.
steps.hint: The sound shrinks. The beat stays the same.

steps.guide: Follow the loudness signs. Keep your steady beat.
steps.caption: Soft → loud. Speed does not change.
steps.prompt: Can soft music still be fast?
steps.hint: Loudness and speed are separate choices.

study.title: Change the loudness
study.teach: Dynamics tells how loud or soft to play. It does not change the written pitches, rhythms, or tempo.
study.example: Play the same C quietly, then loudly. Its pitch stays C. You can repeat the same rhythm at the same speed.
study.prompt: A tune keeps its notes and speed but gets softer. What changed?
study.hint: Louder or softer means a change in dynamics.

checks.prompt: A melody stays on C but grows louder. Which element changes?
checks.hint: Dynamics can change while pitch stays the same.

checks.prompt: A melody keeps the same speed but becomes softer. Which element changes?
checks.hint: Softer sound is a change in dynamics.

study.title: Soft and loud
study.teach: Piano means soft and uses p. Forte means loud and uses f.
study.example: As an instruction, piano means soft, even when another instrument plays it. Changing f to p makes the music softer.
study.prompt: Which instruction asks for a loud sound?
study.hint: Forte means loud. Its sign is f.

checks.prompt: What does p ask you to play?
checks.hint: p means soft. It changes loudness, not the note letters.

checks.prompt: Which marking means “soft”?
checks.hint: Use p for soft.

study.title: Very soft still makes a sound
study.teach: Pianissimo, pp, means very soft. Fortissimo, ff, means very loud. Very soft is different from silence.
study.example: Play gently for pp. A rest tells you to make no sound. For ff, play very loudly while keeping a clear, controlled sound.
study.prompt: Does pp mean complete silence?
study.hint: Pianissimo is a very soft sound. A rest means silence.

checks.prompt: What does pp ask you to play?
checks.hint: pp means very soft. It changes loudness, not the note letters.

checks.prompt: Which marking means “very soft”?
checks.hint: Use pp for very soft.

study.title: Meet the middle levels
study.teach: Mezzo means medium or moderately. Mezzo piano, mp, is moderately soft; mezzo forte, mf, is moderately loud.
study.example: mp and mf sit between the soft and loud ends. mf is louder than mp, but neither means an exact amount of force.
study.prompt: Which full name belongs to mf?
study.hint: m means mezzo. f means forte: moderately loud.

checks.prompt: What does mp ask you to play?
checks.hint: mp means medium soft. It changes loudness, not the note letters.

checks.prompt: Which marking means “medium soft”?
checks.hint: Use mp for medium soft.

study.title: Climb the loudness ladder
study.teach: From softer to louder, the ladder is pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff. Move right to get louder.
study.example: mp is softer than mf. f is softer than ff. For pp, mf, p, put them in this order: pp → p → mf.
study.prompt: Which order goes from softer to louder?
study.hint: Find each mark on pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff, then move from left to right.

checks.prompt: Which is louder: pp or p?
checks.hint: From softer to louder: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff.

checks.prompt: Which is softer: pp or p?
checks.hint: From softer to louder: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff.

study.title: Grow the sound
study.teach: Crescendo means gradually louder. Its hairpin opens wider from left to right. The speed can stay the same.
study.example: Start p, then let the sound grow toward f over several notes. Do not speed up unless another instruction changes the tempo.
study.prompt: What does this widening hairpin ask you to do?
study.hint: A crescendo opens wider as the sound grows.

checks.prompt: Start pp (very soft), then crescendo. What should change?
checks.hint: A crescendo changes loudness gradually.

checks.prompt: Start p (soft), then crescendo. What should change?
checks.hint: A crescendo changes loudness gradually.

study.title: Let the sound fade
study.teach: Decrescendo and diminuendo both mean gradually softer. The hairpin closes from left to right. Keep counting the beat.
study.example: Start f, then gradually fade toward p. The notes keep their written lengths, and the beat stays even unless the tempo changes.
study.prompt: Which word also means gradually softer?
study.hint: Diminuendo and decrescendo both describe a sound getting softer.

checks.prompt: Start pp (very soft), then decrescendo. What should change?
checks.hint: A decrescendo changes loudness gradually.

checks.prompt: Start p (soft), then decrescendo. What should change?
checks.hint: A decrescendo changes loudness gradually.

study.title: Keep the other parts steady
study.teach: Changing loudness does not automatically change speed, pitch, or note lengths. You can change one thing at a time.
study.example: A singer repeats the same phrase more quietly. The notes need not become shorter, and the steady beat need not become slower.
study.prompt: Does a decrescendo automatically mean slow down?
study.hint: Decrescendo changes loudness. Ritardando is the instruction for gradually slowing down.

checks.prompt: A melody stays on C but grows louder. Which element changes?
checks.hint: Dynamics can change while pitch stays the same.

checks.prompt: A melody keeps the same speed but becomes softer. Which element changes?
checks.hint: Softer sound is a change in dynamics.

study.title: Listen to the whole group
study.teach: Dynamics depends on the music around you. Listen so everyone can be heard, and keep loud playing clear and controlled.
study.example: Two instruments both read mf. They may use different effort to balance their sounds. If you cover a quiet solo, play more softly.
study.prompt: You cannot hear the solo because your part is too loud. What can help?
study.hint: Balance means listening to the other musicians as well as yourself.

checks.prompt: A singer is too loud to hear a quiet solo underneath. Which change could help?
checks.hint: Changing dynamics can help musicians balance their sounds.

checks.prompt: Is forte a request to make an ugly or painful sound?
answers: No, aim for a clear controlled loud sound
Yes, always bang as hard as possible
checks.hint: A loud dynamic still needs control and listening.

study.title: Arrive at the next sign
study.teach: A new dynamic tells you the next loudness. Finish a crescendo at its marked destination instead of growing louder forever.
study.example: The music goes p, then crescendo, then f. Begin softly, grow gradually, and arrive at forte. Follow any new sign after that.
study.prompt: A crescendo reaches f. Should you keep getting louder forever?
study.hint: The written f is the loudness you were growing toward.

checks.prompt: A composer wants a sudden strong entrance. Which marking fits better?
checks.hint: Forte asks for a loud sound.

checks.prompt: A composer wants a very gentle entrance. Which marking fits better?
checks.hint: Pianissimo asks for a very soft sound.

tempo.title: Tempo: fast & slow
tempo.intro: Find the beat’s speed, then learn how that speed can change.

steps.guide: Tempo means how fast or slow the beat goes.
steps.caption: Same tune. Same loudness. Different speed.
steps.hint: Tempo changes how quickly the beats arrive.

steps.guide: BPM means beats per minute.
steps.caption: 60 BPM: one beat each second. 120 BPM: twice as many.
steps.prompt: Which has more beats in one minute?
steps.hint: 120 beats is twice as many as 60 beats.

steps.guide: Largo and Adagio are words for slow tempos.
steps.caption: Largo: broad and slow. Adagio: slowly.
steps.prompt: Which word suggests a slow tempo?
steps.hint: Adagio means slowly. Presto is very fast.

steps.guide: Andante feels like walking. Moderato means a moderate pace.
steps.caption: These words guide the feel, not one exact BPM.
steps.prompt: Which word suggests a walking pace?
steps.hint: Walk along with Andante.

steps.guide: Allegro is lively and fast. Presto is very fast.
steps.caption: Exact speeds can vary with the music.
steps.hint: Presto is the very fast word.

steps.guide: Accelerando means get faster little by little.
steps.caption: The beats move closer together. Loudness stays the same.
steps.hint: Accelerando speeds up the beat.

steps.guide: Ritardando means get slower little by little.
steps.caption: The beats spread apart. Loudness stays the same.
steps.hint: Ritardando slows down the beat.

steps.guide: Choose speed and loudness separately.
steps.caption: Tempo = speed. Dynamics = loud or soft.
steps.hint: To change tempo, change speed while keeping loudness.

study.title: Meet tempo
study.teach: Tempo means how fast or slow the steady beat goes. It does not mean loud or soft.
study.example: Tap a slow, even beat. Now tap an even beat a little faster. You changed the tempo.
study.prompt: What does tempo tell us?
study.hint: Tempo is the speed of the beat.

checks.prompt: You tap a slower steady beat. Compared with a faster beat, the taps are…
checks.hint: A slower tempo leaves more time between the steady beats.

checks.prompt: The beats stay at the same speed, but you play more loudly. Did the tempo change?
answers: No, the speed of the beat stayed the same
checks.hint: Tempo is speed, not loudness. A louder sound can keep the same tempo.

study.title: Feel the beat underneath
study.teach: A metronome gives steady beat clicks. Tempo is their speed. Rhythm is the changing pattern of note lengths.
study.example: Keep tapping the steady beat while a tune uses long and short notes. Short notes can fit over slow beats; fast beats can continue under a held note.
study.prompt: Must a busy rhythm always have a fast tempo?
study.hint: The note pattern can be busy while the steady beat stays slow.

checks.prompt: A steady drum pulse continues while the singer uses long and short notes. Which part stays even?
checks.hint: The beat is the even pulse underneath changing rhythms.

checks.prompt: A melody has a busy rhythm. Must its tempo be fast?
checks.hint: Many short notes can fit over a slow steady pulse.

study.title: Words for a slow pace
study.teach: Largo means very slow and broad. Adagio means slow. Both guide the pace of the beat.
study.example: A wide, very slow opening suits Largo. A slow, unhurried tune suits Adagio. These words describe speed, not loudness.
study.prompt: Which word suggests a very slow, broad opening?
study.hint: Largo is the very slow, broad word.

checks.prompt: What does Largo suggest?
checks.hint: Largo is a tempo word meaning very slow and broad.

checks.prompt: Which tempo word means “very slow and broad”?
checks.hint: Largo suggests very slow and broad.

study.title: Walking and moderate pace
study.teach: Andante means at a walking pace. Moderato means at a moderate pace: neither especially slow nor especially fast.
study.example: Imagine walking comfortably for Andante. Moderato suggests a middle pace. The music and its metronome marking help choose the exact speed.
study.prompt: Which word suggests a walking pace?
study.hint: Walk with Andante. Moderato is a moderate pace.

checks.prompt: What does Andante suggest?
checks.hint: Andante is a tempo word meaning at a walking pace.

checks.prompt: Which tempo word means “at a walking pace”?
checks.hint: Andante suggests at a walking pace.

study.title: Lively and very fast
study.teach: Allegro means fast and lively. Presto means very fast. Tempo words suggest a pace, not one fixed BPM for every piece.
study.example: Allegro can suit a lively dance; Presto can suit a very fast chase. Neither word changes note letters or tells you an exact loudness.
study.prompt: Which word suggests very fast music?
study.hint: Presto is very fast. Allegro is fast and lively.

checks.prompt: What does Allegro suggest?
checks.hint: Allegro is a tempo word meaning fast and lively.

checks.prompt: Which tempo word means “fast and lively”?
checks.hint: Allegro suggests fast and lively.

study.title: Read beats per minute
study.teach: BPM means beats per minute. With the same beat note, a bigger number means a faster beat.
study.example: A metronome at 80 BPM makes 80 beats in one minute. With the same beat note, 120 BPM is faster than 80 BPM.
study.prompt: For the same beat note, which is slower: 72 BPM or 144 BPM?
study.hint: The smaller number gives fewer beats each minute, so they arrive more slowly.

checks.prompt: For the same beat unit, which tempo is faster: 60 or 72 BPM?
checks.hint: For the same note unit, more beats per minute means a faster pulse.

checks.prompt: For the same beat unit, which tempo is slower: 60 or 72 BPM?
checks.hint: For the same note unit, more beats per minute means a faster pulse.

study.title: Speed up little by little
study.teach: Accelerando means gradually faster. The beats move closer together. Loudness stays the same unless another sign changes it.
study.example: Like a train gathering speed, the pulse moves from slow to faster over several beats. You can do this softly or loudly.
study.prompt: The music says accelerando. What should happen?
study.hint: Accelerando changes the speed of the beat, not its loudness.

checks.prompt: The music begins Largo, then says accelerando. What should happen?
checks.hint: Accelerando changes speed upward; ritardando changes speed downward.

checks.prompt: The music begins Adagio, then says accelerando. What should happen?
checks.hint: Accelerando changes speed upward; ritardando changes speed downward.

study.title: Slow down little by little
study.teach: Ritardando means gradually slower. Let the beats spread farther apart smoothly, rather than stopping or skipping them.
study.example: At the end of a tune, the pulse gently relaxes. Ritardando describes that slowing, not a quieter sound.
study.prompt: Which instruction asks for gradually slower beats?
study.hint: Ritardando slows the beat. Crescendo and pianissimo describe loudness.

checks.prompt: The music begins Largo, then says ritardando. What should happen?
checks.hint: Accelerando changes speed upward; ritardando changes speed downward.

checks.prompt: The music begins Adagio, then says ritardando. What should happen?
checks.hint: Accelerando changes speed upward; ritardando changes speed downward.

study.title: Go back to the earlier speed
study.teach: A tempo means return to the earlier main speed after a tempo change.
study.example: Start at 100 BPM, then slow down. When you see a tempo, return to 100 BPM: the speed before the slowing.
study.prompt: Your earlier speed was 80 BPM. After slowing, a tempo means return to…
study.hint: Return to the earlier speed, not a doubled or halved speed.

checks.prompt: Which instruction best describes “a tempo” after a change in speed?
answers: Return to the earlier main speed
checks.hint: A tempo restores the earlier main tempo.

checks.prompt: You follow “a tempo” and return to the earlier speed. What should you do next if there is no new speed instruction?
answers: Keep that earlier main speed steady
checks.hint: Return to the main speed and keep it steady until another instruction changes it.

study.title: Fit beats into seconds
study.teach: At 60 BPM, one beat takes one second. At 120 BPM, each beat takes half a second.
study.example: At 30 BPM, beats are farther apart: one beat takes two seconds. At 60 BPM, tap once each second. At 120 BPM, tap twice each second.
study.prompt: At 30 BPM, about how long is one beat?
study.hint: There are 60 seconds in a minute. Thirty beats fit when each takes two seconds.

checks.prompt: At 60 BPM, about how long is one beat?
checks.hint: There are 60 seconds in a minute, so 60 beats fit at one per second.

checks.prompt: At 120 BPM, about how long is one beat?
checks.hint: 120 beats fit into 60 seconds: two beats each second.

study.title: Count a group of beats
study.teach: Find a group’s time by adding the time each beat takes. You can count beats instead of rushing.
study.example: 60 BPM: four beats last four seconds. 120 BPM: four beats last two seconds. At 120 BPM, two beats fit in each second.
study.prompt: At 120 BPM, how many beats fit in two seconds?
study.hint: Two beats fit in one second. Another two fit in the next second: four altogether.

checks.prompt: At 60 BPM, about how long do four beats last?
checks.hint: Each beat takes one second, so four beats take four seconds.

checks.prompt: At 120 BPM, about how long do four beats last?
checks.hint: At two beats per second, four beats take two seconds.

study.title: Read the note beside the number
study.teach: A metronome marking needs a note and a number. The note shows what gets each click; the number gives BPM.
study.example: Half note = 60 means each click is one half-note beat. Quarter note = 60 uses quarter-note beats. The number alone does not tell the whole story.
study.prompt: A marking says half note = 60. Which note gets each click?
study.hint: Read the pictured note first, then read how many of those beats fit in a minute.

checks.prompt: A metronome marking shows a half note = 60. Which note gets each click?
checks.hint: Read the note shown next to the number: that note is the beat unit.

checks.prompt: Two markings both say 80, but one uses quarter-note clicks and one half-note clicks. Is the beat unit important?
answers: No, numbers tell the whole story
checks.hint: The number and the chosen note unit both matter.

study.title: Change speed and loudness separately
study.teach: Tempo changes speed; dynamics changes loudness. They can change separately or together when both instructions appear.
study.example: Ritardando plus decrescendo means slower and softer. Accelerando plus crescendo means faster and louder. A crescendo alone does not tell you to speed up.
study.prompt: Ritardando and decrescendo happen together. What changes?
study.hint: Ritardando slows down. Decrescendo gets softer.

checks.prompt: A tune grows louder with no tempo instruction. Should its beat automatically speed up?
checks.hint: Loudness and tempo can change independently.

checks.prompt: A tune becomes softer with no tempo instruction. Should its beat automatically slow down?
checks.hint: Soft sound can keep the same tempo.

accidentals-key-signatures.title: Accidentals & key signatures
accidentals-key-signatures.intro: Learn one pitch-changing sign at a time, then read key signatures.

sections.title: A local sign lasts for its bar
Key signatures, time signatures & shared notes

study.title: Find the very next key
study.teach: A half step moves to the very next piano key. Count black keys as well as white keys.
study.example: C → C-sharp is one half step. C-sharp → D is another. Do not jump over a black key.
study.prompt: Which key is one half step above C?
study.hint: The black key between C and D is C-sharp.

checks.prompt: Starting on C-sharp, which key is one half step higher?
checks.hint: C-sharp and D are neighboring piano keys.

checks.prompt: How many half-step moves take you from C through C-sharp to D?
checks.hint: C to C-sharp is one move. C-sharp to D is a second move.

study.title: Join two small steps
study.teach: A whole step is two half steps. Move to the next key twice.
study.example: C → C-sharp → D is one whole step. The black key counts as the first small step.
study.prompt: How many half steps make a whole step?
study.hint: One small step plus another small step makes a whole step.

checks.prompt: Start on C and move to the next key twice. Where do you finish?
checks.hint: Move C → C-sharp → D. Two half steps make one whole step.

checks.prompt: A player forgets to count C-sharp between C and D. What should they do?
checks.hint: Each move goes to the very next key, including the black key.

study.title: Some white keys are neighbors
study.teach: E and F are a half step apart. B and C are also a half step apart.
study.example: There is no black key between E–F or B–C. The very next key can be white; half steps do not always end on black keys.
study.prompt: Is E → F a half step or a whole step?
study.hint: E and F are neighboring piano keys, with no key between them.

checks.prompt: How far apart are neighboring B and C?
checks.hint: There is no black key between B and C; one move reaches the next key.

checks.prompt: Can a half-step move land on a white piano key?
answers: Yes; E to F is an example
No; it must land on black
Only if you skip a key
checks.hint: A half step means the next key, whatever its colour.

study.title: A sharp goes higher
study.teach: A sharp sign, ♯, raises a note by one half step. It changes pitch, not loudness.
study.example: Put ♯ before C to play C-sharp: the very next piano key higher than C.
study.prompt: What does a sharp do?
study.hint: Sharp means one half step higher.

checks.prompt: C receives a sharp sign. What name do you use for its changed pitch?
checks.hint: Keep the note’s letter C and add sharp: C-sharp.

checks.prompt: A sharp sign appears before a note. Must you also play that note louder?
checks.hint: Sharp raises the note by one half step. It does not set loudness.

study.title: A flat goes lower
study.teach: A flat sign, ♭, lowers a note by one half step.
study.example: E-flat is the very next piano key below E. Keep its letter name E and add flat.
study.prompt: Where is E-flat compared with E?
study.hint: Flat means one half step lower.

checks.prompt: Which letter stays in the name E-flat?
checks.hint: Keep the letter E and add flat to show its lower pitch.

checks.prompt: Adding a flat to a note changes its pitch or its beat count?
checks.hint: Flat lowers the pitch by one half step. The written note length stays the same.

study.title: A natural cancels a change
study.teach: A natural sign, ♮, cancels a sharp or flat for that note. Return to its natural letter pitch.
study.example: C-sharp changed C higher. A natural before C cancels that change, so play C natural.
study.prompt: Which sign cancels a sharp or flat?
study.hint: The natural sign is ♮. It cancels an earlier sharp or flat.

checks.prompt: C-sharp is cancelled by a natural sign. What do you play?
checks.hint: The natural sign cancels the sharp and restores C.

checks.prompt: An E-flat receives a natural sign. Which pitch is restored?
checks.hint: A natural cancels a flat as well as a sharp; E-flat returns to E natural.

study.title: Notice where the signs sit
study.teach: A local accidental sits before a note. A key signature sits after the clef and before the time signature.
study.example: The shaded sign after this treble clef is the key signature. The sharp beside the later C belongs to that note.
study.prompt: Where does the key signature go?
answers: After the clef, before the time signature
study.hint: Read clef, then key signature, then time signature.

checks.prompt: A sharp sits immediately before one note. What kind of sign is it?
checks.hint: A local accidental belongs beside a note; a key signature follows the clef.

checks.prompt: Which sign comes first when reading clef, key signature, and time signature?
checks.hint: Their order is clef → key signature → time signature.

study.title: One sharp: change every F
study.teach: A key signature with one F-sharp tells you to play F-sharp whenever an F appears.
study.example: G major uses this one-sharp signature. Its notes are G A B C D E F-sharp G.
study.prompt: With this signature, an F normally sounds as…
study.hint: The F-sharp in the signature changes the F notes.

checks.prompt: The signature changes F to F-sharp. Does it also make C sharp?
checks.hint: A one-sharp signature names F-sharp. Other letters stay unchanged unless another sign changes them.

checks.prompt: Which major key in the example uses this one-sharp signature?
checks.hint: G major uses the signature with one F-sharp.

study.title: One flat: change every B
study.teach: A key signature with one B-flat tells you to play B-flat whenever a B appears.
study.example: F major uses this one-flat signature: F G A B-flat C D E F.
study.prompt: Which note does this signature change?
study.hint: The signature shows B-flat.

checks.prompt: The signature changes B to B-flat. Does it also change E to E-flat?
checks.hint: Only B is named in this one-flat signature.

checks.prompt: Which major key in the example uses this one-flat signature?
checks.hint: F major uses the signature with one B-flat.

study.title: A signature can change two letters
study.teach: A key signature can contain more than one sign. Two sharps here change F and C.
study.example: D major uses F-sharp and C-sharp. Its notes are D E F-sharp G A B C-sharp D.
study.prompt: Which notes change with this two-sharp signature?
study.hint: Read both signs: F-sharp and C-sharp.

checks.prompt: D major’s signature changes F and C. Does that signature also sharpen D?
answers: No; D stays natural unless changed locally
checks.hint: The two signs name F-sharp and C-sharp, not D-sharp.

checks.prompt: Which note list follows the D-major key signature?
answers: D E F G A B C D
D-sharp E F G A B C D
D E F-sharp G A B C-sharp D
checks.hint: Use both named changes: F-sharp and C-sharp.

study.title: Keep the signature at every height
study.teach: A key signature applies to its named letters at every octave. Keep using it until the key signature changes.
study.example: An F-sharp signature changes both a lower F and a higher F. A new bar does not erase the key signature.
study.prompt: Does an F-sharp key signature apply to a higher F too?
answers: Yes, every F unless changed locally
study.hint: The key signature follows the letter name at every height.

checks.prompt: A new bar begins but the F-sharp key signature has not changed. What should happen to F?
checks.hint: A bar line does not erase the key signature.

checks.prompt: The key signature changes to one with no sharps or flats. What should you do next?
answers: Keep using the old F-sharp signature
checks.hint: A signature stays in force until a different key signature replaces it.

study.title: A local sign lasts for the bar
study.teach: A local accidental changes that pitch at the same octave for the rest of its bar.
study.example: The first F has a sharp. The later Fs at that same height stay sharp in this bar, even without another sign.
study.prompt: After a local F-sharp, what happens to another F at the same height in that bar?
study.hint: Keep the local change for the same pitch and octave until the bar line.

checks.prompt: A local F-sharp appears at one height. Does it automatically sharpen F in another octave?
answers: No; the local sign applies to that pitch and octave
checks.hint: A local accidental applies to the same pitch at the same octave for the rest of its bar.

checks.prompt: Without another sign, how long should you keep that local F-sharp at the same height?
answers: For the rest of that bar
checks.hint: Keep the local change through that bar, up to the bar line.

study.title: The next bar follows the signature
study.teach: At the next bar, a local accidental ends. Follow the key signature again.
study.example: Here there is no key signature. A local F-sharp lasts in its bar. After the bar line, F returns to F natural.
study.prompt: With no key signature, what does F become in the next bar?
study.hint: The local sharp ends at the bar line. The empty signature means natural F.

checks.prompt: What marks the end of a local accidental’s usual effect?
checks.hint: At the next bar, return to the key signature.

checks.prompt: With no key signature, an E-flat was local to the last bar. What does E use in the new bar?
checks.hint: The local flat ended at the bar line; no signature change is left on E.

study.title: A natural can override the signature
study.teach: A local natural can cancel a signature’s sharp for the bar. The signature returns in the next bar.
study.example: The signature says F-sharp. A natural before F makes it F natural in this bar. In the next bar, F-sharp returns.
study.prompt: After this bar ends, what does the next F normally become?
study.hint: The temporary natural ends. The F-sharp key signature still applies.

checks.prompt: The signature says F-sharp, but a local natural appears before F. What do you play in this bar?
checks.hint: The local natural temporarily cancels the signature’s sharp for that pitch.

checks.prompt: Does that local natural erase the F-sharp key signature for the whole piece?
answers: Yes; every F is flat now
checks.hint: The natural is local to the bar. The F-sharp signature returns in the next bar.

study.title: Two signatures, two jobs
study.teach: The key signature changes note pitches. The time signature organizes beats into bars.
study.example: One sharp changes F to F-sharp. The nearby 4/4 does a different job: four quarter-note beats in each bar.
study.prompt: Which signature tells you how beats fit in a bar?
study.hint: Time signatures organize musical time; key signatures change pitch names.

checks.prompt: Which instruction changes F’s pitch in a one-sharp, 4/4 example?
checks.hint: The key signature handles pitch; the time signature handles beats.

checks.prompt: What does the nearby 4/4 organize in that example?
answers: Four quarter-note beats in each bar
checks.hint: The time signature tells you how the beats fit in a bar.

study.title: The same notes can have different homes
study.teach: C major and A natural minor both use no sharps or flats in their key signatures. Their home notes differ.
study.example: Both use these white-key notes: A B C D E F G. C major comes home to C. A natural minor comes home to A.
study.prompt: Does an empty key signature always mean the home note must be C?
answers: No: A natural minor shares it
It means there are no notes
study.hint: Shared notes do not force the same home note.

checks.prompt: A natural minor has no signs in its key signature. Which note is its musical home?
checks.hint: A natural minor and C major share notes, but A natural minor comes home to A.

checks.prompt: C major uses the same white-key notes. Which home note makes it C major?
checks.hint: The note collection can stay the same while the home changes. C major comes home to C.
